title: Engaged Buddhism
hookLine: practice put to work for peace, justice and the earth

cards: Bombs are falling near a village. In the temple, the monks and nuns face a question no rulebook settles: stay in the meditation hall and keep the practice, or go out and help the wounded?
A Vietnamese Zen teacher, Thich Nhat Hanh, told this story for years afterward, and his answer was neither one. Both. Go out and help, and keep the practice while you do it.
Breathe while you carry the stretcher. That answer has a name now.

teach.b: Day one thousand nineteen told that story first; today, its travels. First, the name. The phrase engaged Buddhism is closely tied to Thich Nhat Hanh and the war years in Vietnam.
It means practice that doesn't stop at the meditation hall door: the attention you bring to a breath, you bring to a hungry neighbor, a broken law, a cut-down forest. Second, the old root.
Engaged Buddhists don't say they invented anything.

They point back to the Buddha's teaching on compassion, karuna, the wish that someone's suffering would end, and to lines like this one from the Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation: "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love—this is an old rule."
Engaged Buddhists take that old rule into protests, peace talks and courtrooms. Third, the many forms.
In Sri Lanka, a village movement called Sarvodaya brings neighbors together to build roads and dig wells, and treats the shared work as practice.

In Thailand, some monks have wrapped orange robes around old trees, ordaining them, so that cutting them down feels like harming a monk. Elsewhere, engaged Buddhists work on prisons, poverty and the climate.

teach.h: A CALM MIND IS PART OF THE WORK.
teach.b: Engaged teachers say anger dressed up as justice burns people out, and a calm mind is part of the work, not a break from it.
Not every Buddhist teacher puts the weight in the same place: some say inner work comes first and action flows from it; others say the two can't be pulled apart.
What engaged Buddhists share is the picture from the village: the stretcher in your hands, the breath in your chest.

how: Engaged Buddhists bring meditation and the teaching on compassion into social work, peace work, village development and care for the earth, often treating the work itself as practice.

games.q: you're a monk in a temple near the fighting. bombs are falling on the village. what do you do?
o: stay in the meditation hall and keep practicing.
leave the practice behind and go help.
go out and help, and keep the practice while you do.
games.why: in the story Thich Nhat Hanh told, the answer is both: carry the stretcher, and keep breathing mindfully as you carry it.

practice: Let the breath settle, and bring to mind one small thing in your world that needs a hand: a neighbor who's struggling, a littered street, a cause you've meant to look up.
Don't solve it yet; just breathe with it, the way the monks breathed with the stretcher. Then let one act small enough to really do come to mind, and keep breathing with it there.

wordCard.voice: Engaged Buddhism. Buddhist practice put to work in the world, for peace, justice and the earth, with the calm of the meditation hall carried into it. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit karuna: compassion, the wish that another's suffering would end.

carryVoice: Your line: practice in action. The calm goes with you out the door. See you tomorrow.
